title: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)
objectives: Define a large language model and explain what 'large' and 'language model' each mean.
Describe the next-token prediction objective that every modern LLM is built on.
Distinguish base (pre-trained) models from instruction-tuned and chat models.
Compare well-known LLM families, open-weight versus closed models, and their trade-offs.
List the core capabilities and limitations of LLMs that interviewers expect you to know.
definition: A Large Language Model (LLM) is a deep neural network, almost always a Transformer, trained on a very large amount of text to predict the next token in a sequence. Because it has billions of parameters and has seen a vast range of text, it can follow instructions, answer questions, summarise, translate, reason over text and write code by generating one token at a time.

theory.heading: What a language model is
theory.body: A language model assigns probabilities to sequences of text. Given 'The capital of India is', it should assign a high probability to ' New' and then ' Delhi'. Early language models were n-gram counters that only looked at the previous one or two words. Neural language models, and especially Transformers, look at the whole preceding context, which lets them capture grammar, facts, style and long-range meaning.
points: Core task: predict the probability distribution of the next token given the previous tokens.
Text is generated by repeatedly choosing a token and appending it to the input (autoregression).
The same simple objective, at scale, produces surprisingly general abilities.

theory.heading: What makes it 'large'
theory.body: 'Large' refers to three things growing together: parameters (from hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions or more), training data (trillions of tokens of web pages, books, code and papers) and compute (thousands of GPUs for weeks). Scaling-law research showed that loss falls predictably as these grow, and that bigger models trained on more data show new abilities such as following instructions and multi-step reasoning.
points: Parameters are the learned weights of the network.
Training data is measured in tokens, not words or documents.
Scale improves capability but raises cost, latency and energy use.

theory.heading: Base models, instruction-tuned models and chat models
theory.body: A base model is the result of pre-training alone: it continues text but does not reliably follow instructions. Instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs) teaches it to respond helpfully. Preference tuning, such as RLHF or DPO, further aligns answers with human preferences for helpfulness and safety. Chat products such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini use instruction- and preference-tuned models, often called 'instruct' or 'chat' variants.
points: Base model: great at continuing text, useful for further fine-tuning.
Instruct/chat model: follows instructions and conversational formats.
Alignment adds safety behaviours such as refusing harmful requests.

theory.heading: The LLM landscape
theory.body: Closed models (OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini) are accessed through APIs; you cannot download their weights. Open-weight models (Meta Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Google Gemma, DeepSeek) can be downloaded and run on your own hardware, fine-tuned and deployed privately, subject to their licences. The choice depends on quality needs, data privacy, cost, latency and in-house ML skills.
points: Closed APIs: strongest general quality, no infrastructure, data leaves your network.
Open weights: full control, private deployment, fine-tuning, but you run the infrastructure.
Small language models (a few billion parameters) can run on laptops or phones for narrow tasks.

theory.heading: Capabilities and limitations
theory.body: LLMs are strong at language tasks: drafting, summarising, extracting fields, classifying with instructions, translating, explaining and generating code. They have a knowledge cut-off date, cannot see your private data unless you provide it, can hallucinate, may reflect training-data bias and are limited by their context window. Most production patterns in this course (RAG, tools, guardrails, evaluation) exist to work around these limitations.
points: Knowledge cut-off: no awareness of events after training unless given in the prompt.
Non-determinism: the same prompt can give different answers when sampling is used.
Context window: only a limited number of tokens can be considered at once.

example.title: A base model versus a chat model
example.body: Give the same text to a base model and an instruction-tuned model. The base model treats it as a document to continue, so it may produce another question. The chat model treats it as a request and answers. The snippet uses the Hugging Face pipeline with a small open model; exact outputs vary by model and version.

code.source:
from transformers import pipeline

# A small base model just continues the text
base = pipeline('text-generation', model='gpt2')
print(base('What is the capital of France?', max_new_tokens=20)[0]['generated_text'])
# e.g. 'What is the capital of France? What is the capital of Germany? ...'

# An instruction-tuned chat model answers the request
chat = pipeline('text-generation', model='Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct')
messages = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is the capital of France?'}]
print(chat(messages, max_new_tokens=20)[0]['generated_text'][-1]['content'])
# e.g. 'The capital of France is Paris.'

demonstration.description: Watch next-token prediction at work. A model looks at the context and assigns probabilities to candidate next tokens; the chosen token is appended and the process repeats. The probabilities below are illustrative.

code.source:
Context: "The Taj Mahal is located in"
Candidate next tokens and probabilities:
  " Agra"   0.86
  " India"  0.09
  " the"    0.03
  " Delhi"  0.01

demonstration.output:
Step 1 picks " Agra" -> "The Taj Mahal is located in Agra"
Step 2 predicts "," then " Uttar", " Pradesh", "." -> "The Taj Mahal is located in Agra, Uttar Pradesh."

takeaways: An LLM is a large Transformer trained to predict the next token on massive text data.
Generation is autoregressive: predict, append, repeat.
'Large' means more parameters, more training tokens and more compute.
Base models continue text; instruction- and preference-tuned models follow requests.
Closed API models and open-weight models trade convenience against control and privacy.
Know the limits: knowledge cut-off, hallucination, bias, non-determinism and context length.

interview.question: What is a Large Language Model?
interview.answer: A large neural network, usually a Transformer, trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token. At scale this lets it understand and generate language: answering, summarising, translating and writing code.
interview.explanation: Mention the Transformer architecture, the next-token objective and scale. Avoid saying it 'understands like a human'; describe it as learned statistical patterns.

interview.question: What is the difference between a base model and an instruction-tuned model?
interview.answer: A base model is only pre-trained to continue text. An instruction-tuned model is further fine-tuned on instruction-response examples, and often preference-tuned with RLHF or DPO, so it follows requests and behaves safely.
interview.explanation: Strong answers name the training stages (pre-training, SFT, preference tuning) and when you would pick a base model (as a starting point for custom fine-tuning).

interview.question: Open-weight or closed-API model: how would you choose for an enterprise project?
interview.answer: Consider data privacy and compliance, required quality, cost at expected volume, latency, need for fine-tuning and team skills. Closed APIs are fastest to start; open weights give control and on-premise deployment.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want a trade-off discussion, not a brand preference. Mention that many teams prototype with an API and later move high-volume or sensitive workloads to open models.

interview.question: Why does an LLM not know about yesterday's news?
interview.answer: Its knowledge comes from training data collected up to a cut-off date; the weights do not update during use. To answer about recent events you must provide the information in the prompt, for example with search or RAG.
interview.explanation: Connects a limitation to its standard fix (retrieval or tools), which shows system thinking.

interview.question: Why can the same prompt give different answers?
interview.answer: The model outputs a probability distribution, and decoding usually samples from it with temperature or top-p. Different samples produce different text. Setting temperature to 0 (greedy decoding) makes output far more repeatable, though not always bit-identical across hardware.
interview.explanation: Links non-determinism to decoding, which Day 5 covers in detail. Mentioning the hardware caveat shows practical experience.

practice.title: Generate text with a bigram language model
practice.objective: Experience next-token prediction and autoregressive generation with the simplest possible language model.
practice.statement: Build a bigram model from a training corpus: for every pair of consecutive words, count how often the second word follows the first. Then generate text greedily: start from a given word and, up to k times, append the word that most often follows the current last word. Break ties by choosing the alphabetically smallest word. Stop early if the current word was never followed by anything in the corpus. Words are the lowercase, whitespace-separated pieces of the corpus.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: the corpus (one line of text).
Line 2: the start word.
Line 3: k, the maximum number of words to generate.
practice.output_format:
Line 1: the generated text (start word plus generated words, separated by single spaces).
Line 2: generated=<number of words added>

example.input:
the cat sat on the mat the cat ate the fish
the
4
example.output:
the cat ate the cat
generated=4

constraints: The corpus has at least one word; 0 <= k <= 50.
Lowercase the corpus and the start word before use.
practice.starter:
from collections import defaultdict

words = input().lower().split()
start = input().strip().lower()
k = int(input())

counts = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))
# TODO: count bigrams, then generate greedily
practice.solution:
from collections import defaultdict

words = input().lower().split()
start = input().strip().lower()
k = int(input())

counts = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))
for a, b in zip(words, words[1:]):
    counts[a][b] += 1

output = [start]
for _ in range(k):
    followers = counts.get(output[-1])
    if not followers:
        break
    best = min(followers.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))[0]
    output.append(best)

print(' '.join(output))
print(f'generated={len(output) - 1}')
explanation: Lowercase and split the corpus, then zip the list with itself shifted by one to visit every consecutive pair.
Store counts in a nested dictionary: counts[current][next] = frequency. This is the model's 'learned parameters'.
To generate, look up the followers of the last word and pick the one with the highest count; sorting by (-count, word) breaks ties alphabetically.
Append the chosen word and repeat, exactly like an LLM appends its predicted token; stop when there is no known follower or k words were added.

quiz.question: What objective are LLMs pre-trained on?
options: Predicting the next token given previous tokens
quiz.explanation: Pre-training uses next-token prediction on huge text corpora; other abilities emerge from this objective at scale.

quiz.question: You send 'Explain recursion' to a base model and it replies 'Explain iteration. Explain closures.' Why?
options: A base model continues text instead of following instructions
quiz.explanation: Base models are trained only to continue text. Instruction tuning is what makes models answer requests.

quiz.question: Which pair are both open-weight model families?
quiz.explanation: Meta Llama and Mistral publish downloadable weights; GPT, Claude and Gemini models are accessed through APIs.

quiz.question: A bank cannot send customer data outside its own data centre but wants an LLM assistant. What is the most suitable starting point?
options: An open-weight model deployed on its own infrastructure
A closed API with no agreement
quiz.explanation: Open-weight models can be hosted privately, keeping data inside the bank's network.

quiz.question: What does the 'knowledge cut-off' of an LLM refer to?
options: The maximum length of an answer
The date after which the model's training data contains no information
The number of users allowed per day
quiz.explanation: The model only knows what was in its training data, which was collected up to a certain date.
